messages.subject: Re: overfitting in DSM
messages.body_plain:
Rob:

The gamma parameter constraining the wiggliness of the gam fits is
'hardwired' into the call to the gam function that the Distance
interface makes.  So this penalty is already imposed by Distance.
Perhaps in a future release of Distance the value of gamma could be
selected by the user, but for the moment 1.4 is the value to which this
argument is set.

messages.subject: Re: overfitting in DSM
messages.body_plain:
It's really a problem of fitting gams to spatial data - the problem
occurs when you're extrapolating beyond the range of the data.  (It may
not be obvious in terms of (x,y) coords that you're doing this - it may
be some odd or extreme combination of values of other covariates in
those grid cells.)  We're developing approaches which provide more
robust extrapolation, but they're not yet available in Distance.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: overfitting in DSM
messages.body_plain:
Hi List,

Personally I think the maximum number of degrees of freedom allowed
to a potential explanatory variable should reflect how plausibly
bendy the analyst thinks the relationship could be. The default for
gams is 10 knots, 9 degrees of freedom. Is the response of whales say
to depth for example really likely to be a curve  that uses 9 degrees
of freedom? I typically constrain my curves to a maximum of 5 or 6
knots, perhaps more if some purely spatial variable like Lat or Lon
is being used but never now the gam default of 10. This can be
implemented as s(Depth,k=5) in writing the model formula. This still
gives considerable flexibility.

thanks

Charles

messages.subject: Re: change transect length
messages.body_plain:
Paulo:

Transect length needs to accurately reflect the amount of effort
expended in the survey.  I worry that you might adjust transect length
to remove sections of transect where effort was expended but nothing was
seen.  That would badly bias the estimated density or abundance.

The information about transect length you provide to the software must
be the amount of transect surveyed.

messages.subject: Re: Decimals and ceros
messages.body_plain:
Elisa:

If you are using the data import 'wizard' that walks you through the
series of steps necessary to import data from a text file, notice a box
entitled 'Decimal symbol' in Step 4 (where Distance is showing the data
it has found in the text file you specified).  There you can either use
the 'regional settings' (default) or you can override the regional
settings (which are set by your operating system) and specify the use of
'.' as the decimal symbol.

My suggestion is that you select '.' to override the regional settings,
and hopefully this will solve you problem.

messages.subject: [Fwd: Re: [DIST-SAMP] overfitting in DSM]
messages.body_plain:
Rob,

Some thoughts on this problem below, but most of this reply will require
you to tap into R directly (I'm not very familiar with the DSM engine)...

You could also try rescaling your lat and lon values (if you haven't
already) so that they represent the same distance in each direction and
use an isotropic smoother. I would try 'soap' which is a bit more work
as you'll have to specify the boundary, but the examples are useful and
easy to follow (tip: use locator() and manually click round the boundary
if your boundary is quite high resolution - problems can occur if your
boundary is too detailed). In any case, using the soap-film smoother
might help with your unreasonably high edge values.  What error
distribution are you using? It might be worth trying the Tweedie
distribution which is readily  available in mgcv, and experiment with
the p-parameter. (See ?Tweedie within the mgcv package for more details.)

Is your 'ice' value a concentration, or a 'distance from'? Are you
hitting problems due to latitude and ice essentially measuring the same
thing? I wonder about trying a tensor product of te(ice, lon)... (given
that you probably want 'ice' in your model, and not just spatial
co-ordinates?)

In summary, this sort of thing is not necessarily a problem just due to
overfitting... check you are fitting a half-decent model as well! :-)

Some (perhaps useful) things to help with this, which I use fairly
routinely (but still don't always get a good model fit!):

(1) 'gam.check' within mgcv
(2) Choice of k: value not too critical as the smoothing parameters
control the model complexity, BUT if too small you will oversmooth, and
if too large, then computations may take too long. Quick check on
whether you've chosen a large enough k is to extract the deviance
residuals from the full model, and to smooth these w.r.t. x using a
Normal model and larger k. If the smooth picks up a pattern in the
residuals, then k should be increased in the original model. (See
'choose.k' in mgcv)
(3) usual residual checking (plot(model,residuals=T) and residuals(model) )

Cheers,
Sharon.

Rob Williams wrote:
> > Hi all,I am fitting a spatial model in Distance 6.0 (Release 2).  I'd like to fit a model of the form
> > ~te(lon,lat)+s(ice)
> > The model appears to be overfitting.  It's very wiggly, and is predicting unreasonably high density at the edges of the survey area where ice concentration is very high or very low.
> > Is there a way to call "gamma=1.4" in dsm within Distance to avoid overfitting?  (I'm getting "unused argument" or "unexpected ",") error messages, so I definitely have the syntax wrong if it is.)  Does this argument require me to run dsm in R?

messages.subject: Re: p-values from GAM
messages.body_plain:
Rikke:

Your finding of low P-values in a fitted gam for many of your covariates
is not that terribly surprising.  It is likely the case that all of
those factors may contribute to where cetaceans are located.  You will
still need to go through a model selection process (using GCV scores)
however to identify the most parsimonious model for your data.

We have not fully implemented all error distributions in the density
surface modelling engine.  If you wish to investigate other
distributions such as the negative binomial, you might be best to work
with the DSM R package inside R.  To learn more about using the negative
binomial in conjunction with fitting a gam, load the mgcv package in R
[library(mgcv)], then request help about the negbin argument to gam
[?negbin]

However, the use of negbin is untested in Distance 6.

messages.subject: Boat survey design for flying birds
messages.subject_clean: Boat survey design for flying birds
messages.body_plain:
Hello

=20

I am designing a boat survey to estimate tern densities. Our survey area
will approximately be a coastal strip c. 40km long out to 20km offshore,
which encompasses the breeding colony. As all birds will be flying, we
are using a snapshot count method (essentially point counts) with
distance bands within a 180 degree arc ahead of the boat, out to 300m.

=20

I would like some advice on the best way to get a systematic random
design for the point counts  for such a boat survey. I was planning to
use the Distance programme to design zig-zag line transects within our
survey area. I was then going to have the point count positions located
at e.g. 1km intervals along the transect. The idea is that the boat will
travel at speed between count points, but slow down to allow the count
to be made instantaneously.

=20

First question is how do I ensure that the point counts are allocated
randomly (but systematic)? Could I randomly assign the first count point
within the first 1km of the transect, and then space them at equal
distance from that one?

=20

Secondly, there will be areas of lower density  further offshore, so I
would like to have less effort (fewer point counts) in this area (to
reduce survey time). Can I simply space the point counts e.g. every 2km
instead of 1km in this area, if so how do I then deal with this reduced
effort during analysis stages?  Or do I first need to split the survey
area into two strata, design the zig-zag transects, and then position
the point counts.=20

=20

Or should I be doing something completely different?!

=20

Thanks

Linda

=20

=20

messages.subject_clean: Boat survey design for flying birds
messages.body_plain:
Linda:

I can appreciate that you'd like your boat to travel in a zigzag for
efficiency, and that you want to do snapshots at regular intervals.
However, if you place your snapshots at fixed distances along the
transects, they probably won't end up being systematic with respect to
each other (because of the zigzag).  Is it impractical to use the
Distance survey design engine (systematic grid sampling) to place a set
of systematic points into your study area, then after that design is
created, connect up the pattern of points in the most efficient manner?

Your second matter about differing amounts of effort at distances
offshore could most simply be addressed by the stratification mechanism
you describe.  I believe the Mexico sample project that comes with
Distance is an example of placing differing amounts of sampling
intensity within different strata.

That's my view, but other design mavens may have more clever ideas.
